title: Velcro's First Version Didn't Work
title_options: The Velcro Patent Nobody Talks About
Velcro Started With Hooks Grabbing Hooks
sources_on_screen: US Air Force AMRL report, Jan 1963

beats.say: Velcro's first design had no loops at all. Just hooks, grabbing other hooks.
beats.vis: Two strips, both bristling with hooks, pressed together; most hooks slide past each other.

beats.say: In nineteen fifty-one, a Swiss inventor, George de Mestral, applied for a patent on it.
beats.vis: Patent page US 2,717,437 drawn in the glow style; the stamp 'Switzerland, 22 Oct 1951'.

beats.say: The story goes that burrs stuck to him on a day outdoors, and he wondered why they held on so well.
beats.vis: Burrs on a coat sleeve. ARTISTIC: a dog may appear in the background, but the voice never mentions it (C024). No alpine peaks (C022, C033): woods and fields near a lake.

beats.say: A burr is covered in tiny hooks.
beats.vis: Dive into the burr: hooked tips. No hook count on screen (M6).

beats.say: So he made hooks out of nylon. Loop a thread over a hot metal bar, so it keeps its shape. Then snip one side. The loop becomes a hook.
beats.vis: Patent Fig. 1 animated: thread loops over a bar, the bar glows, a knife in the groove cuts one side, a hook springs up.

beats.say: He called it a velvet type fabric. Press two pieces together, and the hooks grab each other.
beats.vis: Patent Fig. 2: two hook pieces face to face, turned slightly.

beats.say: But most of them missed. His own later patent says only about thirty percent of the hooks caught.
beats.vis: A grid of hooks; 3 in 10 light up as caught, 7 in 10 grey. '~30%'.

beats.say: So in nineteen fifty-seven, he changed one side. Hooks on one strip. Soft loops on the other. About a thousand loops in every square centimetre, so far more hooks find something to grab.
beats.vis: The bottom strip turns into a dense loop field; hooks drop in and almost all light up. '1 cm²: ~1,000 loops'.

beats.say: And a 2015 study found that Velcro's hooks work less like a burr's, and more like those of a different plant.
beats.vis: Burr hook (needle-like) beside a Velcro hook; a question mark becomes a small woodland plant. The plant name stays off screen until C028's name source is found.

beats.say: By nineteen sixty-three, the US Air Force had stuck it to an aircraft's ceiling, so people in loop-soled gym shoes could try to walk on it while weightless.
beats.vis: Cut-away plane; a person upside down on a hook-lined ceiling track, gym shoes with loop soles.
beats.src_line: US Air Force AMRL report, Jan 1963

beats.say: NASA used it all through Apollo to hold equipment in place. NASA didn't invent it. A Swiss inventor did.
beats.vis: Astronaut gear patched with strips; small stamp 'NOT a NASA invention'.

beats.say: It started with hooks that missed. Would you have kept going?
beats.vis: Back to the two hook strips from b01; they peel apart and the desk drawer closes.
